🔥🇲🇽 <u>Lozoya's mansion now belongs to the Mexican people</u>

The Supreme Court threw out Emilio Lozoya's final appeal, making his 51-million-peso mansion in Lomas de Bezares property of the nation — a house the former Pemex director bought with bribe money from magnate Alonso Ancira and Odebrecht cash funneled through a shell company. The neoliberal looting is being reversed one seized property at a time.

🇲🇽💪 <u>Mexican wages just hit 30.8% of GDP — their biggest slice of the economy in decades</u>

INEGI reports worker pay climbed to 30.8% of Mexico's GDP in Q1 2026, up 4.1 points since 2018, as total labor income jumped 9.4% year-on-year to 10.9 trillion pesos. Six years of minimum-wage hikes are doing what four decades of neoliberalism only ever promised.

<u>US MEDIA</u>: 🔇 García Luna's seized millions now fund Mexico's poorest schools
August 28, 2026 | 💀

📰 A Miami court forced García Luna's US frontmen — the Weinberg family — to liquidate 12 Florida properties. Mexico recovered $5.8M and is sending every peso to schools in Guerrero's Montaña, one of the country's poorest regions.

US outlets ran García Luna's conviction for years. The recovered money reaching Indigenous classrooms got zero US coverage.

• "Around 100 million pesos going to [one of] the most disadvantaged areas in the country." — Sheinbaum

🇲🇽📊 <u>Mexico's public finances came in stronger than the crisis critics forecast</u>

Mexico closed the period through July with a primary budget surplus of 13 billion pesos — against a projected deficit — as VAT collection grew 9.9% in real terms, its strongest run since 2021, and oil revenue rose 10.7%, per Hacienda. Public debt held at 51.5% of GDP, below the programmed level and enough to preserve the country's investment grade and favorable financing conditions.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Mexico, the only country invited abroad, teaches the US how to fight corruption</u>

Mexico was the sole international guest at the US National Association of State Auditors, Comptrollers and Treasurers (NASACT) annual conference, where its Anti-Corruption and Good Governance Ministry presented a model of fighting graft through citizen participation — 'preventing corruption also means building citizenship.' The country whose officials Washington once lectured is now the one being asked to teach.

🇲🇽🛡️ <u>Mexico dismantles a migrant-trafficking cell that ran tunnels into the US</u>

Mexican federal forces — the Navy, the FGR and the Public Security Ministry — captured Ana Florella Fragoso Ramos, alias 'Tía,' and four associates in Jalisco, a 'La Nueva Empresa' cell that smuggled migrants through tunnels from Ciudad Juárez into the United States alongside kidnapping and extortion. Raids in Zapopan and Tonalá seized two vehicles, cash, 31 phones and three payment terminals — the network's logistics laid bare.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>Mexico launches its 2nd National Plan on Women, Peace and Security</u>

Mexico has rolled out its Second National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security (2026–2030), coordinating six federal bodies — Interior, Foreign Affairs, Defense, Navy, the Women's Ministry and Public Security — to guarantee women's 'full, equal, meaningful and safe' participation in security and peacebuilding under UN Resolution 1325. Six years into a feminist foreign policy, Mexico is one of the few nations turning the slogan into an interagency mandate.

🇲🇽💰 <u>Mexico froze 24,662 accounts and 8.7 billion pesos in criminal money</u>

Mexico's Financial Intelligence Unit has blocked 24,662 bank accounts tied to 2,395 people and frozen 8.679 billion pesos since October 2024, UIF chief Omar Reyes reported — nearly one in three accounts directly linked to organized crime, with 1,443 more frozen under the national anti-extortion strategy launched in July 2025. Mexico City, Jalisco, Nuevo León and Sinaloa topped the map — a cartel-finance dragnet run entirely through Mexican institutions.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>17 Mexicans dead in Trump's ICE machine — Mexico is filing charges</u>

Mexico's Foreign Ministry has filed 20 formal complaints — 12 before US district prosecutors, 8 before state prosecutors — over the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals under ICE custody or during raids since Trump took office, 14 of them while detained. Foreign Secretary Roberto Velasco says the UN High Commissioner referred all 17 cases to the Human Rights Council for independent review — a response that stands in sharp contrast to the silence from US authorities.
